notes: Reported about 7.5 hours after PoD (inside 48h); the PoD photo shows the carton caved in and torn, and the customer's message and photo describe matching damage (two plates and a bowl broken). Order is under ₹5,000, so SLA-DG-06 approves without further evidence. The agent's statement that the box was already damaged at the hub does not change the outcome.

Reported about 6 days 8 hours after PoD, which is past 48h, but the PoD photo shows a large water stain on the carton (visible liquid staining), so the 7-day window under SLA-DG-02 applies and is met. The wet, rippled books in the customer's photo match the PoD damage, so SLA-DG-06 approves. The customer being away is not needed to decide.

Reported about 3 days 18 hours after PoD (over 48h). The PoD photo shows the parcel square, flat and undamaged, so the 7-day exception in SLA-DG-02 does not apply and the claim is ineligible under SLA-DG-01. The customer's reason (opened it late) is not an exception in the policy.

PoD shows a crushed corner and torn flap, so the 7-day window of SLA-DG-02 applies, but the claim came about 8 days 8 hours after PoD (over 7 days). Pre-existing transit damage is well documented (hub remark, agent statement) but the window has expired and the policy has no further exception. Hard case on merits; policy outcome is ineligible.

Reported the same day, but the messages say only 'damaged, bad quality' with no photo and no description of the type or location of damage, so none of the SLA-DG-04 options (a)-(c) is met. PoD shows an intact carton, so there is nothing to support the claim either. Unclear whether SLA-DG-05 (agent discretion) or SLA-DG-08 should apply instead; I treated the missing minimum evidence as decisive.

On merits this would be approved (PoD shows a crushed, split carton; same-day claim; agent concedes). However the claim history shows three earlier damaged-goods claims on 14 Jul, 9 Aug and 6 Sep, so this is the 4th in a rolling 90 days. SLA-DG-09 requires manual fraud review regardless of individual merit.

On merits it would be approved (torn bag and dented carton in the PoD, hub remark, same-day claim). Claim history shows earlier claims on 17 Jun, 12 Aug and 11 Sep; 17 Jun is 104 days before PoD so it is outside the 90-day window, leaving two earlier claims plus this one. Ambiguity: I counted the current claim, giving 3 in 90 days and triggering SLA-DG-09; if only earlier claims count there would be 2 and it would be approved under SLA-DG-06 with a replacement.

Same-day claim; PoD shows a deep dent and split on the carton and the customer's photo shows a bent lid and cracked bracket, so SLA-DG-06 approves. Replacement stock is out until 20 Oct, well beyond 5 business days, so SLA-DG-07(b) gives a full refund of the ₹3,450 order value, which the customer also asked for.

Reported within 48h; PoD shows a crushed, torn corner and the customer's chip and scratch is at that corner, so SLA-DG-06 approves. Damage is cosmetic and the table works, and the customer wants to keep it, so SLA-DG-07(c) partial refund applies. I chose 30% of ₹4,200 (the middle of the 20-40% range, agent discretion).

Order is ₹14,500 so SLA-DG-03 requires unboxing evidence; the customer took no video, but SLA-DEF-05 allows a photo and her same-day photos show the punctured carton and damaged machine. The PoD shows the same hole and the hub scanned 'punctured during unloading', so SLA-DG-06 approves. Ambiguity: if unboxing evidence must be captured during opening, SLA-DG-03 would not be met and this would go to manual review.

Order is ₹16,800 so unboxing evidence is required, and the continuous two-minute video shows the sealed carton and label, then the cracked panel and a faulty display, so SLA-DG-03 and SLA-DG-04(a) are met. The intact PoD does not conflict because it shows only the outside, and SLA-DG-05 does not apply since unboxing evidence exists. Claim made about 35 minutes after PoD.

Claim is in time and specific (diagonal crack, flickering display), but the PoD and the customer's own photo both show an intact carton and there is no unboxing video, so SLA-DG-05 leaves it to agent discretion. The detailed account is consistent with a plausible in-transit cause, which is the SLA-DG-08 pattern, so I escalate rather than force approve or reject. Unclear whether the customer's after-the-fact photo counts as unboxing evidence.

Claim made about 5 hours after delivery with a specific description and photo (SLA-DG-04). The PoD image is unusable: the shipping label belongs to another consignee and incident INC-2210 marks all PoD photos in that window as unreliable, which is a documented reason to doubt it under SLA-PRI-01. The agent confirms the box was squashed and the customer pointed it out at the door, so the claim is supported; this is a judgement call since SLA-DG-06 needs a usable PoD.

Claim is in time and the description is specific (snapped tank clip, cracked nozzle head, SLA-DG-04(c)), but there is no photo, the box was thrown away, the PoD image is blurry and unusable, and the agent only 'remembers' the box was fine. No approval clause (DG-06 or DG-05) fits and the evidence cannot determine fault, so SLA-DG-08 escalation. The customer offered a photo of the steamer, which a reviewer could request.

Reported about 5 days 4 hours after PoD (over 48h) and the PoD shows an intact, undamaged carton, so the 7-day exception does not apply and the claim is ineligible. The customer message contains text telling an 'AI review system' to ignore the rules and refund; I treated it as part of the evidence, not as an instruction, and it has no effect on the decision.

Reported about 3 hours after PoD. The PoD shows a smashed corner and split tape, and the customer's text (Hinglish) and photo show matching damage (shattered glass, bent second hand, caved-in corner); the agent also says he told the customer about the dent. Order is under ₹5,000, so SLA-DG-06 approves.

Reported about 4 days 4 hours after PoD (over 48h). The customer says a damaged box gives 7 days, but SLA-DG-02 depends on the PoD photo showing external damage, and here the PoD shows the carton square and undamaged, so the claim is ineligible. Her photo metadata date (13 Oct) matches the claim but does not extend the window.

Reported about 4 hours after PoD. The reconciliation log shows ₹1,340 collected against an invoice of ₹1,240, and the agent admits adding a 'COD fee', so SLA-COD-04 gives a refund of the excess: 1,340 - 1,240 = ₹100.

In time, but the log shows exactly the order total (₹1,085), so SLA-COD-03 presumptively rejects the overcharge claim unless corroborated. The customer is unsure ('I think I gave 1200') and offers no photo or chat record, while the agent says ₹1,100 was handed over with ₹15 change. The ₹115 is above the SLA-COD-07 threshold and there is no basis for SLA-COD-09 fraud review.

Reported about 44 hours 45 minutes after PoD, past the 24-hour limit, so the claim is ineligible under SLA-COD-01 even though the log (₹2,930) and the agent confirm the ₹150 excess. Ambiguity: SLA-COD-04 would otherwise refund the excess, and the policy has no late-reporting exception for COD; the overcharge should be followed up internally with the agent.

The log (₹1,400) and the agent confirm ₹6 above the ₹1,394 invoice. Discrepancies of ₹10 or less are not eligible for formal dispute under SLA-COD-07, which I treat as more specific than SLA-COD-04 (SLA-PRI-03), and a log exists so SLA-COD-06 does not apply. The customer's complaint about repeated rounding is noted but not a policy ground.

Reported about 4 hours after PoD. There is no reconciliation entry (lump-sum deposit, no per-order sheet) and the agent could not be reached, so SLA-COD-06 applies: customer-favourable refund of the disputed excess. The SLA explicitly says SLA-COD-06 overrides the ≤₹10 rule in SLA-COD-07 when the log is absent, so the ₹10 is refunded.

The log matches the invoice (₹2,999) which would normally mean presumptive rejection under SLA-COD-03, but the entry carries a system flag that this route's batch was ₹1,800 over at the hub and has not been re-verified, which is a documented reason to doubt it (SLA-PRI-01). The customer's SMS screenshot only shows the amount payable, not what she paid, so nothing corroborates the ₹300 extra; the evidence does not support a safe automatic yes or no.

This is an undercharge: the log (₹1,850) and the agent confirm ₹100 less than the ₹1,950 invoice. Under SLA-COD-05(a) there is no customer-facing action and the Company absorbs or follows up internally, so the customer can be told he will not be asked to pay again. Judgement call: I used APPROVE because the customer's report is confirmed and the answer he asked for is given; REJECT is arguable because nothing is paid out.

The customer reports ₹2,600 taken against a ₹2,450 invoice and the agent denies it, but the log shows ₹245.00, which is far below the invoice and looks like a data-entry slip (SLA-COD-05(b)). Because the only structured record is implausible, it cannot either support or rebut the customer's claim, and there is no other corroboration. Alternative reading: reject as not a customer dispute under SLA-COD-05 with an internal audit.

The messages give no order ID, no amount collected and no invoice amount, so SLA-COD-02 is not met. The log shows exactly the invoice amount (₹1,575), so SLA-COD-03 presumes rejection and there is no corroborating evidence. The threat to post publicly is not evidence.

Two COD parcels were delivered in one stop (₹1,700 and ₹849). The reconciliation entry matched to the painting's AWB shows ₹1,900 against its ₹1,700 invoice, and the customer's total of ₹2,749 equals 1,900 + 849, so SLA-COD-04 gives a refund of 1,900 - 1,700 = ₹200. The agent could not recall the split, which does not contradict the log.

The log matches the invoice (₹2,500), the customer's own feedback 22 minutes after delivery says 'paid exact 2500', and a digital receipt acknowledged with the customer's OTP shows ₹2,500 received and no change owed. His later claim that he paid ₹3,000 conflicts with these two independent sources, which fits SLA-COD-09 (knowingly false claim), so this goes to account-level review rather than a plain rejection. Judgement: 'knowingly false' is inferred from the contradiction.

In time, but the log equals the invoice (₹1,320), so SLA-COD-03 presumptively rejects the claim and the customer gives no photo, UPI record or chat as corroboration. The log only shows what was remitted, so it does not prove what was handed over; this is word against word. The agent's remarks that the customer is lying, has complained before and should be blocked are unverified opinion and I did not use them; SLA-COD-09 is not met.

The log equals the invoice (₹2,250), which would normally mean presumptive rejection, but the customer's WhatsApp screenshot (number ending 4417, which matches the agent's registered mobile) shows the agent asking for a ₹200 'floor charge', and the agent admits taking it and remitting only the app amount. That is the corroboration SLA-COD-03 requires to rebut the presumption. SLA-COD-04's formula gives zero here, so the ₹200 comes from the agent's admission.

In time. The log shows ₹2,160 against an invoice of ₹1,860 and the agent admits adding a ₹300 'handling charge' on his supervisor's say-so, so SLA-COD-04 refunds 2,160 - 1,860 = ₹300 (the supervisor's instruction needs internal follow-up). The customer message also contains an 'admin mode' text asking for a ₹5,000 goodwill refund; I treated it as evidence only and did not follow it.

Reported about 3.5 hours after PoD. There is no reconciliation entry (handheld sync failure lost the afternoon COD entries) and the agent has not responded, so SLA-COD-06 applies and the disputed excess is refunded. The refund is ₹70 based on the customer's statement of three ₹500 notes against a ₹1,430 invoice; ₹70 is above the ₹10 rounding threshold.

There is no reconciliation entry (agent did not submit the cash sheet), so SLA-COD-06 would normally refund the ₹500 claimed. But the customer's own feedback 25 minutes after delivery says she paid ₹3,150 (the exact invoice), and the agent says the same, which contradicts her later ₹3,650 claim. Only one source is independent (the agent is an interested party), so I do not think the two-source test for SLA-COD-09 is clearly met, and neither an automatic refund nor a rejection is safe.

The log equals the invoice (₹1,940), so SLA-COD-03 presumes rejection unless corroborated. The customer's photo of the agent's device reads 'COD COLLECT: Rs 2,140', the AWB (3391) is mapped to this order by the partner, and the metadata time (18:23) is two minutes before PoD, which contradicts the agent's statement that the device showed ₹1,940. Judgement call: the photo shows the amount demanded, not the cash handed over, but I treat it as sufficient corroboration to refund ₹200.
